title: Manju Padayatti vs Midhun Jose on 6 November, 2014

paragraphs.text:
IN THE HIGH COURT OF KERALA AT ERNAKULAM

 PRESENT:

 THE HONOURABLE MR.JUSTICE C.K.ABDUL REHIM
 &
 THE HONOURABLE MR. JUSTICE SHAJI P.CHALY

 TUESDAY, THE 19TH DAY OF APRIL 2016/30TH CHAITHRA, 1938

 Mat.Appeal.No. 68 of 2015 ()
 ---------------------------


AGAINST THE JUDGMENT IN O.P.NO.1369/2014 of FAMILY COURT,ERNAKULAM
DATED 06-11-2014.

APPELLANT/PETITIONER:
--------------------

 MANJU PADAYATTI,
 D/O.P.M.POULOSE,
 VILLA NO.1, CHAKOLAS HABITAT,
 NEAR MILMA, EDAPPALLY P.O.,
 KOCHI-682024


 BY ADV. SRI.ROY CHACKO

RESPONDENT/RESPONDENT:
---------------------

 MIDHUN JOSE,
 HOUSE NO.18, PUTHUSSERY HOUSE,
 KALLUPALAM ROAD, ANGAMALY-683 572.


 BY ADV. SRI.SAIBY JOSE KIDANGOOR

 THIS MATRIMONIAL APPEAL HAVING BEEN FINALLY HEARD ON
01-04-2016, ALONG WITH MAT.APPEAL NOS.81 & 103 OF 2015, THE COURT ON
19.04.2016 DELIVERED THE FOLLOWING:


 P.T.O



 C.K. ABDUL REHIM
 &
 SHAJI P. CHALY, JJ.
 --------------------------------------------------
 Mat. Appeal Nos.81, 68 & 103 of 2015
 -----------------------------------------------
 Dated this the 19th day of April, 2016


 JUDGMENT
Shaji P. Chaly, J.

Above Matrimonial Appeals arise from a common

judgment of the Family Court, Ernakulam, dated 06.11.2014 in

O.P.No.2205 of 2012, O.P.No.1369 of 2014 and O.P.No.2204

of 2012 respectively. O.P.No.2205 of 2012 is filed by the

appellant seeking dissolution of marriage under Sec.27 of the

Special Marriage Act r/w Sec.10 of Indian Divorce Act, which

was dismissed by the Family Court. O.P.No.1369 of 2014 was

filed by the respondent under Sec.22 of the Special Marriage

Act, 1954, seeking restitution of conjugal rights, which was

allowed by the Family Court. O.P.No.2204 of 2012 was filed

by the appellant seeking realization of an amount of

Rs.35,06,524/- with 12% interest from the date of suit till

realization, which was partly allowed by the Family Court by

granting a decree to the appellant for an amount of

Rs.40,000/- with 6% interest p.a. from 17.11.2011 till its

realization. The Family Court has disposed of the aforesaid

Mat. Appeal No.68/2015 & conn. cases 2

Original Petitions by its common judgment since the subject

matter of the cases are intrinsically connected. Therefore, we

also propose to dispose of the same by a common judgment.

In order to dispose of the appeals, the facts recited in Mat.

Appeal No.81 of 2015 is narrated and the facts in all the

appeals are almost similar and common and therefore separate

narration of facts are not required. If at all the same is

required, it will be stated wherever it is appropriate.

2. Appellant and respondent are wife and husband

respectively. Their marriage was solemnized in accordance

with provisions of the Special Marriage Act on 02.07.2011.

Thereafter on 16.07.2011 a marriage was solemnized in

accordance with rites and ceremonies prevailing in the Syrian

Catholic community to which the appellant and respondent

belong.

3. At the time of marriage, the respondent was

working at IBM India Projects Ltd., at Bangalore as a Software

Engineer and he was deputed for an assignment to Finland, a

country in Western Europe. On 25.07.2011, the respondent

along with the appellant went to Finland to take up his

assignment. It is contended by the appellant that during the

Mat. Appeal No.68/2015 & conn. cases 3

short period of the parties united as man and wife, appellant

found that respondent was a chronic drunkard and behaved in

a very abnormal manner, under intoxication. That apart, it is

contended that, the respondent was not at all interested in

maintaining a cordial and amicable marital relationship with

the appellant and the appellant stated several incidents in the

Original Petition pointing out the abnormal and unusual

behaviour from a highly educated person and he fails to

discharge his duties as a husband. The attitude and behaviour

of the respondent was unbecoming of a lovable husband,

which under the ordinary circumstances would compel the life

partner to leave the matrimonial home to join her parents.

However, hailing from a traditional Catholic background, which

considered marriage as a Sacramental bond, the appellant and

her parents expected with hope that the respondent would

mend his ways, is the contention.

4. It is the further contention of the appellant that,

reaching Finland, the respondent continued his drinking habits

and used to come home very late in the night, that the

assignment in Finland was short lived, the reasons for which

were not divulged either to the appellant or to her parents.

Mat. Appeal No.68/2015 & conn. cases 4

The deputation came to an abrupt halt on 28.08.2011 and

thereupon the respondent was directed to report duty at

Bangalore, immediately. It is further contended that,

termination of the deputation of the respondent in Finland was

unexpected and out of disappointment and frustration, the

respondent took to severe consumption of alcohol almost, non-

stop from morning to night, thus making the situation

uncontrollable. Even though the appellant tried her level best

by requesting the respondent to return to his normal

professional pursuits by stopping consumption of alcohol, the

request was not heeded by the respondent. On the other

hand, the respondent in inebriated condition abused and ill-

treated the appellant on 24.08.2011, accusing her parents and

family members to be the cause for his misfortune.

Respondent immediately told the appellant to call her parents

in order to take the appellant from Finland and declared that

thereupon his life would be saved. Being fearful of the

situations thus emerged, the appellant telephoned her parents

and conveyed them of the necessity of their visit to Finland

and accordingly the parents of the appellant visited Finland on

06.10.2011 and stayed there for two days with the appellant

Mat. Appeal No.68/2015 & conn. cases 5

and the respondent.

5. The respondent left for Bangalore on 08.10.2011

and thereafter the parents of the appellant stayed back to

extend company to the appellant. They remained there till

20.10.2011 and reached back home on 21.10.2011 along with

the appellant. It is the further contention of the appellant

that, in the meanwhile, the respondent had been making

telephone calls to the appellant most of which were in abusive

language, coupled with threats and admonitions. Appellant

contends that, even allegations of pre-marital relationship with

others were also raised against the appellant. At times, when

father of appellant intervened, he had also faced with abusive

words and admonitions from the respondent. Therefore, it is

the case of the appellant that, the situation was such, it

became very difficult for the appellant to continue her marital

relationship with the respondent. As an attempt to regain

marital harmony, family members of both the parties as well

as some common friends advised the respondent and appellant

to visit 'Santwana' Counselling Centre, managed by the

Congregation of the Mary Immaculate, the CMI Priests.

Accordingly, a priest namely Fr. Varghese Puthussery was

Mat. Appeal No.68/2015 & conn. cases 6

requested to provide counselling to both parties. Counselling

was conducted on 29.10.2011 by Fr. Varghese Puthussery.

After counselling, the priest conveyed to both the parents that

the respondent has decided to give up his drinking habit and

accordingly he requested the appellant to accompany the

respondent to Bangalore. The priest also requested the parties

and their parents to meet him for a review after two weeks.

Even though the appellant was hopeful that respondent will

abide the advise provided by the priest during the course of

counselling, quite contrary to the same, the respondent

continued his alcoholic habits with more vigor, causing deep

mental agony to the appellant. The appellant also contended

that, the respondent on one occasion even went to the extent

of declaring that he would go to court for proving her

relationship with her father, which according to the appellant,

was too much to bear. Even though the appellant vehemently

protested on the said remark made, she was severely beaten

up and abused by the respondent. It is also the contention of

the appellant that physical and mental harassment continued

on all the days when they were living at Bangalore.

Mat. Appeal No.68/2015 & conn. cases 7

6. While the appellant and respondent were at

Bangalore, the mother and sister of the respondent visited

them and even though they were in the know of things, they

fully supported the respondent and brought out new set of

allegations against the appellant. This mentally disturbed the

appellant and at that point of time, the appellant called her

parents and requested them to take her to the parental house,

as she suffered from great mental hardship in living with the

respondent, and also conveyed that she could not any longer

adjust with the respondent to continue a healthy and normal

marital relationship. In accordance with the request made by

the appellant, she was brought back to her parental house.

Thereafter, the respondent came to his house on "work from

home arrangement". During this time, respondent attempted

to call the appellant and repeated his demand for seeking

divorce and wanted to talk to her parents about this subject.

The appellant was invited by the respondent to visit his house

in order to go in pilgrimage to few Churches and for attending

a family function. The said request was repeated by the

mother of the respondent also. It is the contention of the

appellant that, as a dutiful wife, appellant believed the words

Mat. Appeal No.68/2015 & conn. cases 8

and went to the respondent's house in order to comply with

the request made by the respondent. The parents of the

appellant permitted her to leave the parental home on

condition that she would be brought back after the family

function is over. Since even after the day of the function the

appellant did not return and this situation created a suspicion

in the minds of the parents that the respondent had plans to

take the appellant to Bangalore clandestinely, the father of the

appellant immediately went to the residence of the respondent

in order to make necessary enquiries.

7. It is contended that, upon hearing the news of the

visit of the father-in-law, the respondent became very furious

and exhibited certain mannerisms which were very abnormal in

nature. The respondent declared that the father- in-law would

not be permitted to enter the house and he would break his

legs and destroy his car if he dares to do so. That, there was

an unruly and uncontrollable situation when the father of the

appellant visited the house of the respondent, which no father

in his senses would have tolerated. The father of the appellant

in spite of all the unbearable situations that took place, kept

his cool and demonstrated absolute craftsmanship in order to

Mat. Appeal No.68/2015 & conn. cases 9

avoid any catastrophe to the appellant. That apart, it is

contended that the respondent shouted in the presence of the

people present there that he would kill his father-in-law, if he

dare to come to meet the respondent with a request to take

away the appellant. The mother and sister of the respondent

who were present there tried their best to persuade him and

restrain him from proceeding further. When the father of the

appellant reached there, respondent who was in his bed room

after having consumed some tablets and oil applied to his

head, wearing only an undergarment, came out of the bed

room and shouted at the father-in-law who requested the

appellant to accompany him immediately with her belongings.

Infuriated by the said situation, respondent snatched the bag

and threw it away. The respondent slapped the appellant on

her face, forcibly dashed her head against the wall and put her

down on the floor and shouted to his sister to close the door in

order to prevent the appellant from leaving the house. At this

point of time, when the father of the appellant tried to save his

daughter from the clutches of the respondent, respondent gave

a forceful push, consequent to which, appellant's father fell

down on the floor and thereupon respondent brutally kicked

Mat. Appeal No.68/2015 & conn. cases 10

him on his chest. At that point of time, when the father of the

appellant cried aloud for help, respondent's mother entered the

scene and opened the door and let the father and appellant

escape from there and the driver immediately took them to the

parental home.

8. The very next day, the respondent along with a

priest viz. Fr. Jolly went to the residence of the appellant and

tried to impress upon the appellant and her parents that the

respondent was very apologetic to them for whatever

happened on the previous day and sought their pardon for all

the misdeeds committed by him. It is the contention of the

appellant that, the said visit was only a ploy in order to

prevent the appellant and her parents from preferring a police

complaint against the physical assault and abuses made

against them. The respondent even fell at the feet of the

appellant in his attempt to seek pardon and so also with the

parents of the appellant. The priest recited few prayers and

requested both parties to carry on with the matrimonial

relationship in a peaceful and amicable manner and he advised

the parents of the appellant to desist from filing a complaint to

the police, thereby spoiling the career of the respondent. On

Mat. Appeal No.68/2015 & conn. cases 11

account of the request made by the priest and the request

made by the respondent by a further undertaking that no such

incident would arise in future, the appellant and her parents

refrained from preferring a police complaint.

9. But, according to the appellant, later they realized

that the demonstrations of pardon exhibited by the respondent

was hollow in nature and he did not keep up his promise made

in the presence of Fr. Jolly to continue the marital life with

harmony and peace. It is under such circumstances, the

appellant believed that the respondent is totally unreliable,

irresponsible and an insane person who is unfit and

incompetent to live a normal life by discharging duties and

responsibilities expected in a healthy and decent marital

relationship. In the meanwhile, the respondent left for U.K. in

connection with another assignment, without informing the

appellant.

10. It is under such compelled circumstances, the

appellant was constrained to file the Original Petition seeking

dissolution of marriage under Sec.27(d) and (e) of the Special

Marriage Act r/w Sec.10(x) of the Divorce Act.

Mat. Appeal No.68/2015 & conn. cases 12

11. The respondent entered appearance and filed

objection. According to the appellant, the denial made in the

objections was not in accordance with law, by extracting the

averment in its entirety and denying the same in one sentence

"are utter false and hence denied by the respondent". After

extracting the contentions of the appellant in the Original

Petition and after denying the same, the respondent has stated

that the father of the appellant had desired for marital alliance

of his daughter with the respondent for the reason that he had

a decent job and was about to pursue his employment in

Finland. That apart, it is stated that, since his father-in-law

found that the assignment in Finland was terminated, he

became furious. He wanted his daughter to go to the parental

house as a sequel to parting company with the respondent. It

is contended that the father of the appellant acted as a

hindrance to their marital relationship. It is also contended by

the respondent that the parties do not have any serious

differences, but it is only the father of the appellant who wants

to create problems and to put an end to the matrimonial

relationship on account of his prejudice to the respondent.

Mat. Appeal No.68/2015 & conn. cases 13

12. From the pleadings, the Family Court has raised two

points for determination: (1) Whether the petitioner is entitled

to get a decree for divorce on the ground of cruelty? and (2)

Relief and costs?

13. In Mat. Appeal No.68 of 2015, the appellant is

challenging the judgment of the Family Court granting the

decree sought for by the respondent for restitution of conjugal

rights. The contentions of the respondent therein are that,

there are no serious matrimonial disputes existing by and

between the appellant and the respondent, that the

respondent has taken all the contentions raised by him under

his objection in O.P.No.2205 of 2012. That apart it is

contended that, the father of the appellant was instrumental in

causing disruption to the matrimonial harmony and peace of

the appellant and the respondent. It is also contended that

the respondent, his friends and well-wishers had requested the

appellant to come out of the clutches of her father in order to

live a happy and harmonious life. But the appellant declined to

abide by such advises provided. The respondent contended

that he is not ready to put an end to the matrimonial bond

created by and between the appellant and the respondent.

Mat. Appeal No.68/2015 & conn. cases 14

14. The appellant objected to the petition filed by the

respondent seeking restitution of conjugal rights by raising the

contentions she has raised in O.P.No.2205 of 2012 and that

apart, it was contended that it is impossible to lead a peaceful

life with the respondent and further that it is dangerous to live

with him. It is also contended by the appellant that the

petition filed for restitution of conjugal rights is nothing but an

afterthought to counter the demand for dissolution of marriage

raised by the appellant. Therefore, the appellant sought for

dismissal of the said petition. After assimilating the rival

contentions, the Family Court has raised one main point

"whether the respondent is entitled to get a decree for

restitution of conjugal rights?".

15. Mat. Appeal No.103 of 2015, as stated earlier, is

filed by the appellant aggrieved by the refusal of the entire

claims sought for by her, for an amount of Rs.35,06,524/-. The

said Original Petition is filed by the appellant against the

respondent/husband and his mother. The Family Court has

passed a decree in favour of the appellant only for an amount

of Rs.40,000/- which was admitted by the respondent in his

written objection, along with interest at the rate of 6% from

Mat. Appeal No.68/2015 & conn. cases 15

the date of petition till realization. There the contention

advanced by the appellant with respect to the said decree,

apart from the contentions advanced in the petition for

dissolution of marriage are that, though the respondent did not

make any demand for dowry at the time of marriage, after

solemnization of the marriage under the Special Marriage Act ,

the respondent started to show his true colour, that the 1st

respondent approached the father of the appellant with a

request to provide financial help to him and requested to part

with an amount of Rs.12 lakhs for paying off the debt that he

had incurred for constructing a house and for meeting the debt

incurred with respect to marriage of the 1st respondent's sister.

Since the customary form of marriage was due to be

performed within a short period, the appellant and her parents

were having no other choice than to pay the amount. Hence,

Rs.12 lakhs was given to respondents 1 and 2 in the said

Original Petition, on 06.07.2011. It is also the contention of

the appellant that respondent had extracted money from the

appellant in one way or the other. An amount of

Rs.3,25,653/- was there in the Bank Account of the appellant

by way of gift from her parents, the same was withdrawn by

Mat. Appeal No.68/2015 & conn. cases 16

the 1st respondent using the Debit Card of the appellant at the

time when the parties were residing in Finland.

16. That apart it is contended that, the 1st respondent

had taken the appellant for a European tour and at that time

he was using the Debit Card of the appellant and the entire

expenses for the journey and Hotel bills were met from out of

the amount remained in the account of the appellant, using her

Debit Card. That apart, father of the appellant remitted an

amount of Rs.1 lakh in the account of the appellant when the

appellant and respondent required money during their tour

abroad. It is also the contention of the appellant that the

respondent had borrowed an amount of Rs.40,000/- while they

were in Finland from the father of the appellant. A further

claim is put forth by the appellant for an amount of

Rs.1,34,000/- which was said to be paid by the father of the

appellant to one Mr. Arun Aravind, a friend of the 1st

respondent, at the request of the 1st respondent. Another

amount of Rs.20,000/- was also borrowed by the 1st

respondent from the father of the appellant to meet his

immediate needs. Thus, altogether, the appellant is entitled to

get back Rs.18,19,653/- in total from the respondents, was the

Mat. Appeal No.68/2015 & conn. cases 17

contention.

17. In addition to that, according to the appellant, she

and her family have also incurred an amount of Rs.4 lakhs for

conducting the marriage. Apart from the same, appellant

claims an amount of Rs.10 lakhs towards compensation, and

thus totally claiming an amount of Rs.35,06,524/-.

18. Respondent filed objection denying the averments

made with respect to the reasons leading to the filing of the

petition for dissolution of the marriage and also denying

receipt of any amount from the appellant or her parents, apart

from the amount of Rs.40,000/- borrowed by the respondent

from the father of the appellant. After appreciating the rival

contentions, Family Court has raised the issue as to "whether

the appellant is entitled to get a decree for the amount as

sought for by her".

19. Appellant has examined herself as PW1 and marked

Exts.A1 to A2(a), A3 to A7(a) and A8 and A9. Father of the

appellant was examined as PW2. Respondent was examined

as RW1 and a Bank Manager was examined as RW2 and

marked Exts.B1 to B1(n), B2 to B2(h), B3 to B3(i), B4 to B4

(k), B5 to B5(f), B6 to B6(h) and B7 to B20 and B20(a) to

Mat. Appeal No.68/2015 & conn. cases 18

B26.

20. The Family Court after appreciating the rival

contentions and pleadings and the oral and documentary

evidence tendered by the respective parties, has dismissed the

Original Petition filed by the appellant for dissolution of the

marriage, allowed the Original Petition filed by the respondent

for restitution of conjugal rights and partly allowed the Original

Petition filed by the appellant for realization of money. It is

thus challenging the dismissal of the Original Petition for

dissolution of marriage, allowing the petition of the respondent

for restitution of conjugal rights and dissatisfied with the

partial decree for an amount of Rs.40,000/- with interest, the

above appeals are preferred by the appellant.

21. Heard; learned counsel for the appellant and

learned counsel for the respondent. Perused the pleadings,

lower court records and the argument notes provided by the

learned counsel for the respondent.

22. Firstly, we will deal with Mat. Appeal No.81 of 2015,

the decision of which will guide the fate of Mat. Appeal No.68

of 2015. So far as the pleadings of the appellant with respect

to dissolution of marriage is concerned, same is predominantly

Mat. Appeal No.68/2015 & conn. cases 19

narrating the incidents that took place in a very short lived

marriage by and between the appellant and the respondent.

The cruelties alleged by the appellant are both mental and

physical in nature inflicted by the respondent on the appellant

as well as on her father. The question now is whether there is

sufficient evidence on record so as to interfere with the order

passed by the Family Court dismissing the petition for

dissolution. So far as the cruelty part is concerned, the oral

evidence tendered by the appellant and the respondent are

oath against oath. The contentions and pleadings put forth by

the appellant is objected in the written objections filed by the

respondent by extracting the averments contained in the

Original Petition and denying the same altogether by stating

that the above "are utter false and hence denied by the

respondent". Thrust of the contention put forth by the learned

counsel for the appellant is that, the denial so made in the

objections is not at all a denial. The allegations specifically

raised by the appellant is not at all denied in specific terms,

which thus means, same are admitted, is the contention

advanced. In order to find out the nature of the pleadings and

the objection, we perused the plaint and objection in all the

Mat. Appeal No.68/2015 & conn. cases 20

three appeals and it is true that the denial of the contentions

put forth by the appellant is only in the nature as recited

above. The question therefore to be considered is whether

there is a proper denial of the pleadings put forth by the

appellant. In our considered opinion, the pleadings put forth

by the appellant are denied since the pleadings are extracted

and stated that the same is denied as such. We do not think

that such a denial may not be the normal procedure, but

however the same cannot be termed as an evasive denial since

the entire pleadings are quoted and denied together.

Therefore, such a denial cannot be treated as not in

accordance with law.

23. However, question remains is, whether from the

evidence adduced by the parties, there is any sufficient

evidence so as to grant a decree of dissolution of marriage,

reversing the findings of the Family Court. The Family Court

had mostly relied on Ext.B1 series of photographs produced by

the respondent to arrive at a conclusive finding that the parties

led a happy matrimonial life and with the said evidence on

board, it cannot be said that there were severe matrimonial

disputes and discord by and between the appellant and the

Mat. Appeal No.68/2015 & conn. cases 21

respondent. However, the appellant has adduced evidence in

terms of the pleadings put forth by her in the Original Petition.

In the cross-examination of the appellant, even though at

length, nothing was brought out to discredit her testimony in

the chief examination. The specific instances pleaded by the

appellant and deposed in her chief affidavit was not specifically

subjected to cross-examination. The tenor of cross-

examination persuade us to think that the attempt of the

respondent was mostly to non-suit the appellant in her claim

for realization of money. In that view of the matter, even if

the pleadings in the Original Petition can be termed to be

specifically denied by the respondent, during cross-

examination, in our view, nothing was brought out to discredit

the versions put forth by the appellant in chief examination.

That apart, PW2, the father of the appellant has corroborated

fully with the evidence tendered by the appellant, wherever he

had knowledge about the incidents narrated by the appellant.

24. Apart from the same, going through the cross-

examination of PW1, we do not find any cross-examination to

penetrate the allegations of drinking habit, violence and other

untoward incidents took place due to the abnormal behaviour

Mat. Appeal No.68/2015 & conn. cases 22

and attitude narrated by the appellant. According to us, in

cross-examination, instead of attempting to deface the

evidence put forth by the appellant in chief examination, the

respondent has attempted mostly to prove that he was

sufficiently wealthy enough to carry on his life without any aid

or support of the appellant and her parents. That apart, in

cross-examination of PW1, suggestions were made with

respect to the allegations made against the respondent in the

Original Petition which was denied by the appellant.

Furthermore, PW1 has reiterated and explained in cross-

examination with respect to the counselling conducted by Fr.

Varghese Puthussery and visit of Fr. Jolly after the incident

that took place at the residence of the respondent as narrated

in the facts. Therefore, two things are predominant while

evaluating the said circumstances: (1) that in order to go for

counselling, there were severe marital disharmony and discord

by and between the appellant and the respondent. Therefore,

with respect to the averment contained in the Original Petition

and the evidence tendered by PW1 in chief examination

regarding the said aspect, it can only be said to be true in its

nature. Moreover, the counselling so conducted and the visit

Mat. Appeal No.68/2015 & conn. cases 23

of Fr. Jolly at the house of the parental home of the appellant,

are not specifically disputed, because when PW1 offered such

an explanation in cross-examination, there is not even a

suggestion made by the respondent disputing the explanations

so put forth by PW1 in her chief examination. (2) the visit of

Fr. Jolly along with the respondent is specifically pleaded by

PW1, in order to pacify the incident that took place at the

house of the respondent. The said aspect is reiterated in chief

examination and when cross-examined PW1 has explained in

detail the visit of Fr. Jolly to the house of the appellant. In

that context, evidence tendered by the respondent as RW1 is

relevant, because the visit of father of the appellant to the

house of the respondent to take her from there is admitted by

the respondent. But the respondent has put forth a different

case in his evidence by deposing that the father of the

appellant misbehaved to the respondent while he went there to

take the appellant.

25. Therefore, the visit of the father of the appellant on

the specific day referred is clearly established. While

appreciating the said circumstance, if the father of the

appellant misbehaved to the respondent, there was no

Mat. Appeal No.68/2015 & conn. cases 24

occasion for the respondent to visit the house of the appellant

with Fr. Jolly since he has not committed any mistake or

indulged in any illegal activity, according to his version in the

deposition. Therefore, the probability of the visit of the

respondent with Fr. Jolly can be seen as a visit to pacify the

situations which took place at the residence of the respondent

and at the instance of the respondent.

26. The said two instances of counselling by Fr.

Varghese Puthussery and visit of Fr. Jolly to the parental

home of the appellant along with the respondent are

substantive circumstances to arrive at a safe conclusion that

severe matrimonial disputes and discord existed consequent to

the cruelty both mental and physical, which was put forth by

the appellant in the pleadings. So far as the respondent is

concerned, his case is that there are no matrimonial disputes

or such circumstances enabling the appellant to seek

dissolution of marriage. If there were no such situations at all,

what was the occasion for the parties to attend counselling by

Fr. Varghese Puthussery, is the question. Viewed in any

circumstances, by appreciating the rival pleadings and the

evidence tendered by the parties, one can reach a safe

Mat. Appeal No.68/2015 & conn. cases 25

conclusion that the pleadings put forth by the appellant and

the evidence tendered by her can only be probable. This is

more so, because if there was no matrimonial discord or

dispute by and between the parties, there was no occasion for

the parties to go for counselling. It is also to be borne in mind

that it is the specific case of the appellant that they went for

counselling to Fr. Varghese Puthussery on the intervention of

the friends and relatives of the respondent. It is also a

circumstance safely leading to a conclusion that severe

matrimonial disputes and discord existed by and between the

appellant and the respondent. Viewed in that manner, the

blunt denial made by the respondent will not in any manner

deface the pleadings put forth and evidence tendered by the

appellant which is substantiated by evidence tendered by PW2,

her father.

27. Moreover, going by the pleadings and evidence, Fr.

Varghese Puthussery and Fr. Jolly were very well aware of the

disharmony that existed between the appellant and the

respondent. So also, both the priests, going by the tenor of

pleadings and evidence, were very well associated with the

family of the respondent. As contended by the learned counsel

Mat. Appeal No.68/2015 & conn. cases 26

for the respondent, it may be true that going by the provisions

of Evidence Act , a burden is cast upon the appellant to prove

the case put forth by her in the Original Petition. But however,

that does not mean that the evidence tendered by PW1 cannot

be believed without corroborating the same by adducing other

oral evidence. The court has the power and authority to

appreciate the evidence tendered by the appellant alone in

order to grant a relief if the same is found to be cogent and

trustworthy. Under normal circumstances, a prudent petitioner

may not venture in examining witnesses who are not confident

enough to support the case of the petitioner. Moreover, the

pleadings put forth by the appellant show that, the incidents

took place in the presence of family members alone and

therefore by examining the mother and sister of the

respondent, he could have succeeded in establishing his case,

that no such incident took place. In our considered opinion,

the appellant was successful in proving the cruelties alleged by

her by satisfactory evidence and therefore the respondent has

failed to adduce the best evidence available in order to

establish that the specific instances alleged to have taken

place at his house, has actually not taken place. That apart, it

Mat. Appeal No.68/2015 & conn. cases 27

is the quality of evidence that matters, rather than quantity.

28. So also, if the case put forth by the respondent that

there was no matrimonial disharmony or discord, it could have

been easily established by examining the aforesaid priests.

That apart, a serious incident of violence, manhandling etc.

according to the appellant, took place at the residence of the

respondent, which incident in a different fashion is admitted by

the respondent by attributing allegations against the father of

the appellant. The presence of mother and sister of the

respondent in his parental home is admitted. The appellant

has put forth a specific case that she and her father could

escape from the parental house of the respondent after the

said incident, due to the help extended by the mother of the

respondent. Therefore, the mother and sister of the

respondent should have been examined on the side of the

respondent to establish that the incidents specifically narrated

by the appellant did not take place at all, which thus means,

the burden of disproving the satisfactory evidence led by the

appellant shifted at that juncture to the respondent.

29. Apart from all these aspects, to the pinpointed and

specific allegations made by the appellant, the respondent has

Mat. Appeal No.68/2015 & conn. cases 28

not made any contra allegations against the appellant.

Therefore, while appreciating the pleadings and evidence put

forth by the appellant, we are persuaded to think aloud as to

the reason why the appellant wanted to leave the matrimonial

home. Under normal circumstances, a wife will not be inclined

to leave the matrimonial home, especially if the husband is

treating her with love and affection. The case of the

respondent is that there was no occasion for causing any

rupture at all to the marital bondage. On the contrary,

respondent has no case that the appellant misbehaved or

behaved cruelly to the respondent so as to cause any

disharmony to the marriage. That being the situation, without

any severe matrimonial disputes and discord, it cannot be

thought of that, the appellant has left the matrimonial home

without any reason at all.

30. Now we will examine the nature of cruelty that was

inflicted by the respondent on the appellant. Appellant has

stated that the respondent has on one occasion told her that

she had pre-marital relationship with other persons. That

apart, on one occasion respondent has declared that he will go

to court to establish the relationship maintained by the

Mat. Appeal No.68/2015 & conn. cases 29

appellant with her father. These aspects, even though may

have uttered once, it has its own deep impact in the mind of a

person. The same will cause deep-rooted distress and

permanent injury in the mind of the person. That apart, such

statements made by the respondent to the appellant will cause

hindrance to the smooth and harmonious relationship. Above

all these, as we have narrated above, when the appellant's

father went to the house of the respondent to take her back to

her parental house, incidents of physical assault inflicted to the

appellant and her father and abuses showered on them cannot

be termed as trivial or flimsy. The institution of matrimony is

built on confidence, not only by the parties to the marriage,

but also by taking into confidence the love and affection

rendered by the parents of both parties and immediate

relatives. Viewed in that background, the physical and mental

torture inflicted is not only on the appellant, but the

respondent has inflicted the same on the father of the

appellant also, which caused mental distress to the appellant.

These are very vital circumstances which can cause serious

apprehensions in the mind of the appellant to continue the

matrimonial institution by and between the appellant and the

Mat. Appeal No.68/2015 & conn. cases 30

respondent. If the respondent was innocent, against the

allegations made by the appellant, there were several

circumstances enabling him to disprove the same, as we have

noted above. The lethargy and neglect of the respondent to

utilize the opportunity to prove his innocence shows that the

appellant has no much concern for the continuance of the

matrimony also. We also notice that the marriage has become

unworkable.

31. Since we find that the pleadings and evidence are

sufficient enough to advance the claim of the appellant, the

cruelty narrated therein are sufficient enough to the

satisfaction of this court to think that the appellant's

apprehension that due to the matrimonial cruelty meted out

from the respondent, it is dangerous to live with the

respondent.

32. Learned counsel for the appellant has invited our

attention to the judgments of the Apex Court in 'Vijayakumar

Ramachandra Bhate v. Neela Vijayakumar Bhate ' [( 2003)

6 SCC 334], 'Vinita Saxena v. Pankaj Pandit ' [(2006) 3

SCC 778], 'A: Husband v. B: Wife' [2010(4) ILR 427],

'Elizabeth alias Jolly George v. T.G. Andrews ' [2011(3)

Mat. Appeal No.68/2015 & conn. cases 31

KHC 267 (DB)] and 'K.R. Srinivas v. Dharmavaram Sridevi'

[III (2012) DMC 427 (DB)], in order to canvass the proposition

that cruelty is not a static term, it can vary from person to

person and circumstance to circumstance. On going through

principles laid down in the afore-noted judgments, we find that

the general principle is that, if and when there is a deep-rooted

mental distress occurred to any of the spouse, it is a

circumstance enabling the court to order dissolution of

marriage on the ground of mental cruelty. That apart, in those

judgments it is found that, some stray incidents of different

occasions may not constitute a ground for dissolution on the

basis of cruelty. However, we find that in the case at hand,

the duration of marriage was only for a short period. But

however, the word 'length' depends on the circumstances. The

period of marriage may be for a short duration, but if the

mental or physical cruelty continued for a substantial period

during the short period of matrimonial life, same can be

termed as a long and continuous cruelty inflicted by one

spouse against the other during the short period of

matrimonial life.
Mat. Appeal No.68/2015 & conn. cases 32

33. Learned counsel for the respondent has invited our

attention to the judgments of the Apex Court in 'Suman

Kapoor v. Sudhir Kapur ' [(2009) 1 SCC 422] and 'K.

Srinivas Rao v. D.A. Deepa' [Civil Appeal No.1794 of 2013

dated 22.02.2013]. On going through the findings of the Apex

Court in those judgments also, the principles laid down in the

earlier noted judgments are followed with respect to the

physical and mental cruelty, which creates a foundation for

seeking dissolution of the marriage on the said ground.

34. Therefore, definitely there were reasons for the

appellant to leave the matrimonial home. Taking into account

the fact situations and also taking into account the evidence on

record, we are persuaded with reasons to think that the case

put forth by the appellant and evidence let in by examining

herself and her father was trustworthy and believable to arrive

at a safe conclusion that the appellant has proved successfully

to the satisfaction of the court by adducing reasonable and

cogent evidence to secure a decree for dissolution of marriage

on the ground of cruelty. Family Court relied on Ext.B series of

photographs in order to arrive at a conclusion that there was

no matrimonial dispute or discord so as to dissolve the

Mat. Appeal No.68/2015 & conn. cases 33

marriage by and between the parties. In our view the said

findings of the Family Court is not correct since the still

photographs produced is not a material to arrive at a

conclusively finding that there was no cruelty inflicted by the

respondent against the appellant. The photographs only shows

that there were moments, where parties enjoyed leisure but

that by itself is not a conclusive proof to establish that there

was no cruelty at all inflicted by the respondent to the

appellant. In every matrimonial life, there may be such

moments but, such moments captured in still cameras cannot

be pressed into service, to establish conclusively that by

witnessing those photographs it shall be presumed by the

court that the appellant and respondent were living happily

through out. To put it otherwise, Ext.B series photographs may

be relevant evidence, but not conclusive, especially taking into

account the facts and circumstances involved in the case at

hand. Therefore, we are justified in arriving at a conclusion

that the findings rendered by the Family Court with respect to

the petition filed by the appellant seeking dissolution of

marriage cannot be sustained under law. The findings suffer

from the vice of proper appreciation of pleadings and evidence

Mat. Appeal No.68/2015 & conn. cases 34

tendered by the parties in a proper, legal and effective

manner. In that circumstances, we set aside the judgment of

the Family Court, Ernakulam in O.P.No.2205 of 2012 and allow

the said Original Petition and thus dissolve the marriage

between the appellant and the respondent solemnized as per

the provisions of the Special Marriage Act on 02.07.2011 and

the customary marriage which took place on 16.07.2011.

35. Now we proceed to consider Mat. Appeal No.68 of

2015, whereby the Family Court has granted a decree in

favour of the respondent for restitution of conjugal rights. The

Family Court has allowed the said Original Petition on the

ground that the appellant has failed to prove that there were

reasonable cause on the part of the appellant to leave the

matrimonial home and live separated from the husband. We

do not think that much discussion is required to arrive at a

conclusion in the said appeal, in view of the findings rendered

by us in Mat. Appeal No.81 of 2015 by reversing the findings

and conclusions of the Family Court and ordered dissolution of

the marriage. The reasons rendered in the said appeal, for

dissolving the marriage is sufficient enough in order to arrive

at a conclusion that the decree granted by the Family Court to

Mat. Appeal No.68/2015 & conn. cases 35

the respondent for restitution of conjugal rights cannot be

sustained under law in any manner. There existed reasonable

and sufficient ground for the appellant to leave the

matrimonial home, and reside separately from the respondent.

Therefore, we set aside the order of the Family Court,

Ernakulam in O.P.No.1369 of 2014 dated 06.11.2014 and

thereby dismiss the said Original Petition.

36. Mat. Appeal No.103 of 2015, as stated by us earlier,

is an appeal filed by the appellant against the partial decree

granted by the Family Court in her favour. Against the claim

of Rs.35,06,524/-, the Family Court has granted a decree for

an amount of Rs.40,000/- with interest. [Even though in the

body of the judgment, interest is shown as 9%, in the relief

portion, it is shown as 6%]. So far as the pleadings with

respect to the Original Petition claiming money is concerned, it

is the specific case of the appellant herself that the respondent

or her parents did not ask for any dowry. The case of the

appellant is that, after the marriage was solemnized under the

 Special Marriage Act , respondent and his parents demanded

Rs.12 lakhs in order to tide over a financial crisis that came on

their way consequent to construction of the residential building

Mat. Appeal No.68/2015 & conn. cases 36

of the respondent's parental home and also to tide over the

financial situations caused pursuant to the marriage of the

sister-in-law of the appellant. The respondent has tendered

evidence before the Family Court and established that the

construction of the residential building of the respondent was

completed way back in the year 2010 and further the marriage

of the sister-in-law of the appellant also took place prior to the

marriage of the respondent. It is not a case where the

appellant has put forth a contention that towards dowry the

said amount was parted with. But the specific contention is

that the same was provided to tide over the adverse financial

circumstances faced by the respondent consequent to the

house construction and the marriage of the sister-in-law of the

appellant. Therefore, by ordinary evidence, it cannot be

presumed that the respondent has received the said amount.

If the case put forth by the appellant that the said amount was

parted with against the claim of dowry, taking into account the

background and circumstances of the appellant, some sort of

presumption and guess work could have been employed by the

Family Court to arrive at a conclusion with respect to the

claim. But the case put forth by the appellant is that no dowry

Mat. Appeal No.68/2015 & conn. cases 37

was demanded by the respondent or his parents and therefore

the pleadings and the evidence tendered on that account has

to be appreciated strictly in accordance with the stipulations

contained under the Evidence Act . Therefore, it was

incumbent on the part of the appellant to clearly establish with

cogent evidence to the satisfaction of the court, in order to

secure a decree for the said amount of Rs.12 lakhs.

37. In order to establish the pleadings put forth and the

evidence tendered by PW1 and PW2, the document that is

relied on by the appellant is the Bank Account from which it is

seen that the appellant has withdrawn an amount of Rs.12

lakhs. The evidence of withdrawal of Rs.12 lakhs will not

suffice the situation because the evidence required in view of

the pleadings put forth by the appellant is the evidence of

parting with money. The said evidence has not come into

effect even though PW1 and PW2 have tendered evidence and

produced the statement of Bank Account. Yet another aspect

that persuades us to think that the said amount of Rs.12 lakhs

is not parted with by the appellant or her father since, from

the pleadings, evidence and document, it is categoric and clear

that the amount of Rs.12 lakhs was lying in a Bank deposit and

Mat. Appeal No.68/2015 & conn. cases 38

therefore it is the money accounted, and while thinking

prudently, if such a sizable amount was expected to be parted

with by the appellant or her father to the respondent, the

normal course adopted would have been by issuing a cheque in

favour of the respondent or his parents or transfer through

Bank. Therefore, the said reasons specified above inspire

confidence on us to think that the appellant has failed to prove

that the said amount was parted with by the appellant/or her

parents to the respondents. Therefore, the circumstances put

forth by the appellant specifically narrating the reasons for

parting with an amount of Rs.12 lakhs at the request of the

respondent cannot be sustained.

38. So far as the other amounts claimed by the

appellant towards the money expended, withdrawn by the

respondent from the Account of the appellant, while they were

in Finland and in European tour etc. are concerned, appellant

had produced her Credit Card accounts. But that by itself is

not a sufficient evidence to establish that money was taken by

the respondent from the accounts of the appellant or her

father. So far as the money with respect to marriage expenses

met by the appellant also, no substantial proof is forthcoming.

Mat. Appeal No.68/2015 & conn. cases 39

That apart, an amount of Rs.10 lakhs in bulk is claimed

towards damages. First of all, in order to sustain a claim for

damages in the pleadings, separate heads should be shown

with respect to damages suffered by the appellant in various

heads. Moreover, no evidence is forthcoming to establish such

claims made by the appellant. The Family Court, in our view,

has evaluated the entire situations, and the evidence on record

and arrived at a finding that the appellant has failed to

establish that she is entitled to a decree as sought for by her.

However, the Family Court has granted a decree for an amount

of Rs.40,000/- since the said amount is admitted by the

respondent as received from the appellant.

39. Therefore, we do not find any reason to interfere

with the partial decree passed by the Family Court for an

amount of Rs.40,000/-. However, in the body of the petition,

the Family Court has granted 9% interest to the said amount

of Rs.40,000/-, but at the relief portion, only 6% interest is

awarded. Taking into account the facts and circumstances, we

are of the opinion that the interest that was granted by the

Family Court to the said amount of Rs.40,000/- is at the rate

of 9% p.a. from 17.11.2011 till its realization. We order

Mat. Appeal No.68/2015 & conn. cases 40

accordingly. Therefore, the said appeal is dismissed, subject to

the above clarification and modification in the decree.

40. In the result, Matrimonial Appeal Nos.68 of 2015

and 81 of 2015 are allowed and Matrimonial Appeal No.103 of

2015 is dismissed, subject to the clarification with respect to

the interest awarded by the court below.
The parties are directed to suffer their respective costs.
Sd/-

C.K. ABDUL REHIM
 JUDGE

 Sd/-

SHAJI P. CHALY
 JUDGE

APPELLANT/PETITIONER:

 MANJU PADAYATTI,
 D/O.P.M.POULOSE,
 VILLA NO.1, CHAKOLAS HABITAT,
 NEAR MILMA, EDAPPALLY P.O.,

 MIDHUN JOSE,

 THIS MATRIMONIAL APPEAL HAVING BEEN FINALLY HEARD ON
01-04-2016, ALONG WITH MAT.APPEAL NOS.81 & 103 OF 2015, THE COURT ON
19.04.2016 DELIVERED THE FOLLOWING:


 P.T.O



 C.K. ABDUL REHIM
 &
 SHAJI P. CHALY, JJ.

 Mat. Appeal Nos.81, 68 & 103 of 2015
 -----------------------------------------------
 Dated this the 19th day of April, 2016


 JUDGMENT

[p_1] Shaji P. Chaly, J.

[p_2] Above Matrimonial Appeals arise from a common

judgment of the Family Court, Ernakulam, dated 06.11.2014 in

O.P.No.2205 of 2012, O.P.No.1369 of 2014 and O.P.No.2204

of 2012 respectively. O.P.No.2205 of 2012 is filed by the

appellant seeking dissolution of marriage under Sec.27 of the

Special Marriage Act r/w Sec.10 of Indian Divorce Act, which

was dismissed by the Family Court. O.P.No.1369 of 2014 was

filed by the respondent under Sec.22 of the Special Marriage

Act, 1954, seeking restitution of conjugal rights, which was

allowed by the Family Court. O.P.No.2204 of 2012 was filed

by the appellant seeking realization of an amount of

Rs.35,06,524/- with 12% interest from the date of suit till

realization, which was partly allowed by the Family Court by

granting a decree to the appellant for an amount of

Rs.40,000/- with 6% interest p.a. from 17.11.2011 till its

realization. The Family Court has disposed of the aforesaid

Mat. Appeal No.68/2015 & conn. cases 2

Original Petitions by its common judgment since the subject

matter of the cases are intrinsically connected. Therefore, we

also propose to dispose of the same by a common judgment.

In order to dispose of the appeals, the facts recited in Mat.

Appeal No.81 of 2015 is narrated and the facts in all the

appeals are almost similar and common and therefore separate

narration of facts are not required. If at all the same is

required, it will be stated wherever it is appropriate.

[p_3] 2. Appellant and respondent are wife and husband

respectively. Their marriage was solemnized in accordance

with provisions of the Special Marriage Act on 02.07.2011.

Thereafter on 16.07.2011 a marriage was solemnized in

accordance with rites and ceremonies prevailing in the Syrian

Catholic community to which the appellant and respondent

belong.

[p_4] 3. At the time of marriage, the respondent was

working at IBM India Projects Ltd., at Bangalore as a Software

Engineer and he was deputed for an assignment to Finland, a

country in Western Europe. On 25.07.2011, the respondent

along with the appellant went to Finland to take up his

assignment. It is contended by the appellant that during the

Mat. Appeal No.68/2015 & conn. cases 3

short period of the parties united as man and wife, appellant

found that respondent was a chronic drunkard and behaved in

a very abnormal manner, under intoxication. That apart, it is

contended that, the respondent was not at all interested in

maintaining a cordial and amicable marital relationship with

the appellant and the appellant stated several incidents in the

Original Petition pointing out the abnormal and unusual

behaviour from a highly educated person and he fails to

discharge his duties as a husband. The attitude and behaviour

of the respondent was unbecoming of a lovable husband,

which under the ordinary circumstances would compel the life

partner to leave the matrimonial home to join her parents.

However, hailing from a traditional Catholic background, which

considered marriage as a Sacramental bond, the appellant and

her parents expected with hope that the respondent would

mend his ways, is the contention.

[p_5] 4. It is the further contention of the appellant that,

reaching Finland, the respondent continued his drinking habits

and used to come home very late in the night, that the

assignment in Finland was short lived, the reasons for which

were not divulged either to the appellant or to her parents.

Mat. Appeal No.68/2015 & conn. cases 4

The deputation came to an abrupt halt on 28.08.2011 and

thereupon the respondent was directed to report duty at

Bangalore, immediately. It is further contended that,

termination of the deputation of the respondent in Finland was

unexpected and out of disappointment and frustration, the

respondent took to severe consumption of alcohol almost, non-

stop from morning to night, thus making the situation

uncontrollable. Even though the appellant tried her level best

by requesting the respondent to return to his normal

professional pursuits by stopping consumption of alcohol, the

request was not heeded by the respondent. On the other

hand, the respondent in inebriated condition abused and ill-

treated the appellant on 24.08.2011, accusing her parents and

family members to be the cause for his misfortune.

Respondent immediately told the appellant to call her parents

in order to take the appellant from Finland and declared that

thereupon his life would be saved. Being fearful of the

situations thus emerged, the appellant telephoned her parents

and conveyed them of the necessity of their visit to Finland

and accordingly the parents of the appellant visited Finland on

06.10.2011 and stayed there for two days with the appellant

Mat. Appeal No.68/2015 & conn. cases 5

and the respondent.

[p_6] 5. The respondent left for Bangalore on 08.10.2011

and thereafter the parents of the appellant stayed back to

extend company to the appellant. They remained there till

20.10.2011 and reached back home on 21.10.2011 along with

the appellant. It is the further contention of the appellant

that, in the meanwhile, the respondent had been making

telephone calls to the appellant most of which were in abusive

language, coupled with threats and admonitions. Appellant

contends that, even allegations of pre-marital relationship with

others were also raised against the appellant. At times, when

father of appellant intervened, he had also faced with abusive

words and admonitions from the respondent. Therefore, it is

the case of the appellant that, the situation was such, it

became very difficult for the appellant to continue her marital

relationship with the respondent. As an attempt to regain

marital harmony, family members of both the parties as well

as some common friends advised the respondent and appellant

to visit 'Santwana' Counselling Centre, managed by the

Congregation of the Mary Immaculate, the CMI Priests.

Accordingly, a priest namely Fr. Varghese Puthussery was

Mat. Appeal No.68/2015 & conn. cases 6

requested to provide counselling to both parties. Counselling

was conducted on 29.10.2011 by Fr. Varghese Puthussery.

After counselling, the priest conveyed to both the parents that

the respondent has decided to give up his drinking habit and

accordingly he requested the appellant to accompany the

respondent to Bangalore. The priest also requested the parties

and their parents to meet him for a review after two weeks.

Even though the appellant was hopeful that respondent will

abide the advise provided by the priest during the course of

counselling, quite contrary to the same, the respondent

continued his alcoholic habits with more vigor, causing deep

mental agony to the appellant. The appellant also contended

that, the respondent on one occasion even went to the extent

of declaring that he would go to court for proving her

relationship with her father, which according to the appellant,

was too much to bear. Even though the appellant vehemently

protested on the said remark made, she was severely beaten

up and abused by the respondent. It is also the contention of

the appellant that physical and mental harassment continued

on all the days when they were living at Bangalore.

Mat. Appeal No.68/2015 & conn. cases 7

[p_7] 6. While the appellant and respondent were at

Bangalore, the mother and sister of the respondent visited

them and even though they were in the know of things, they

fully supported the respondent and brought out new set of

allegations against the appellant. This mentally disturbed the

appellant and at that point of time, the appellant called her

parents and requested them to take her to the parental house,

as she suffered from great mental hardship in living with the

respondent, and also conveyed that she could not any longer

adjust with the respondent to continue a healthy and normal

marital relationship. In accordance with the request made by

the appellant, she was brought back to her parental house.

Thereafter, the respondent came to his house on "work from

home arrangement". During this time, respondent attempted

to call the appellant and repeated his demand for seeking

divorce and wanted to talk to her parents about this subject.

The appellant was invited by the respondent to visit his house

in order to go in pilgrimage to few Churches and for attending

a family function. The said request was repeated by the

mother of the respondent also. It is the contention of the

appellant that, as a dutiful wife, appellant believed the words

Mat. Appeal No.68/2015 & conn. cases 8

and went to the respondent's house in order to comply with

the request made by the respondent. The parents of the

appellant permitted her to leave the parental home on

condition that she would be brought back after the family

function is over. Since even after the day of the function the

appellant did not return and this situation created a suspicion

in the minds of the parents that the respondent had plans to

take the appellant to Bangalore clandestinely, the father of the

appellant immediately went to the residence of the respondent

in order to make necessary enquiries.

[p_8] 7. It is contended that, upon hearing the news of the

visit of the father-in-law, the respondent became very furious

and exhibited certain mannerisms which were very abnormal in

nature. The respondent declared that the father- in-law would

not be permitted to enter the house and he would break his

legs and destroy his car if he dares to do so. That, there was

an unruly and uncontrollable situation when the father of the

appellant visited the house of the respondent, which no father

in his senses would have tolerated. The father of the appellant

in spite of all the unbearable situations that took place, kept

his cool and demonstrated absolute craftsmanship in order to

Mat. Appeal No.68/2015 & conn. cases 9

avoid any catastrophe to the appellant. That apart, it is

contended that the respondent shouted in the presence of the

people present there that he would kill his father-in-law, if he

dare to come to meet the respondent with a request to take

away the appellant. The mother and sister of the respondent

who were present there tried their best to persuade him and

restrain him from proceeding further. When the father of the

appellant reached there, respondent who was in his bed room

after having consumed some tablets and oil applied to his

head, wearing only an undergarment, came out of the bed

room and shouted at the father-in-law who requested the

appellant to accompany him immediately with her belongings.

Infuriated by the said situation, respondent snatched the bag

and threw it away. The respondent slapped the appellant on

her face, forcibly dashed her head against the wall and put her

down on the floor and shouted to his sister to close the door in

order to prevent the appellant from leaving the house. At this

point of time, when the father of the appellant tried to save his

daughter from the clutches of the respondent, respondent gave

a forceful push, consequent to which, appellant's father fell

down on the floor and thereupon respondent brutally kicked

Mat. Appeal No.68/2015 & conn. cases 10

him on his chest. At that point of time, when the father of the

appellant cried aloud for help, respondent's mother entered the

scene and opened the door and let the father and appellant

escape from there and the driver immediately took them to the

parental home.

[p_9] 8. The very next day, the respondent along with a

priest viz. Fr. Jolly went to the residence of the appellant and

tried to impress upon the appellant and her parents that the

respondent was very apologetic to them for whatever

happened on the previous day and sought their pardon for all

the misdeeds committed by him. It is the contention of the

appellant that, the said visit was only a ploy in order to

prevent the appellant and her parents from preferring a police

complaint against the physical assault and abuses made

against them. The respondent even fell at the feet of the

appellant in his attempt to seek pardon and so also with the

parents of the appellant. The priest recited few prayers and

requested both parties to carry on with the matrimonial

relationship in a peaceful and amicable manner and he advised

the parents of the appellant to desist from filing a complaint to

the police, thereby spoiling the career of the respondent. On

Mat. Appeal No.68/2015 & conn. cases 11

account of the request made by the priest and the request

made by the respondent by a further undertaking that no such

incident would arise in future, the appellant and her parents

refrained from preferring a police complaint.

[p_10] 9. But, according to the appellant, later they realized

that the demonstrations of pardon exhibited by the respondent

was hollow in nature and he did not keep up his promise made

in the presence of Fr. Jolly to continue the marital life with

harmony and peace. It is under such circumstances, the

incumbent on the part of the appellant to clearly establish with

cogent evidence to the satisfaction of the court, in order to

secure a decree for the said amount of Rs.12 lakhs.

[p_40] 37. In order to establish the pleadings put forth and the

evidence tendered by PW1 and PW2, the document that is

relied on by the appellant is the Bank Account from which it is

seen that the appellant has withdrawn an amount of Rs.12

lakhs. The evidence of withdrawal of Rs.12 lakhs will not

suffice the situation because the evidence required in view of

the pleadings put forth by the appellant is the evidence of

parting with money. The said evidence has not come into

effect even though PW1 and PW2 have tendered evidence and

produced the statement of Bank Account. Yet another aspect

that persuades us to think that the said amount of Rs.12 lakhs

is not parted with by the appellant or her father since, from

the pleadings, evidence and document, it is categoric and clear

that the amount of Rs.12 lakhs was lying in a Bank deposit and

Mat. Appeal No.68/2015 & conn. cases 38

therefore it is the money accounted, and while thinking

prudently, if such a sizable amount was expected to be parted

with by the appellant or her father to the respondent, the

normal course adopted would have been by issuing a cheque in

favour of the respondent or his parents or transfer through

Bank. Therefore, the said reasons specified above inspire

confidence on us to think that the appellant has failed to prove

that the said amount was parted with by the appellant/or her

parents to the respondents. Therefore, the circumstances put

forth by the appellant specifically narrating the reasons for

parting with an amount of Rs.12 lakhs at the request of the

respondent cannot be sustained.

[p_41] 38. So far as the other amounts claimed by the

appellant towards the money expended, withdrawn by the

respondent from the Account of the appellant, while they were

in Finland and in European tour etc. are concerned, appellant

had produced her Credit Card accounts. But that by itself is

not a sufficient evidence to establish that money was taken by

the respondent from the accounts of the appellant or her

father. So far as the money with respect to marriage expenses

met by the appellant also, no substantial proof is forthcoming.

Mat. Appeal No.68/2015 & conn. cases 39

That apart, an amount of Rs.10 lakhs in bulk is claimed

towards damages. First of all, in order to sustain a claim for

damages in the pleadings, separate heads should be shown

with respect to damages suffered by the appellant in various

heads. Moreover, no evidence is forthcoming to establish such

claims made by the appellant. The Family Court, in our view,

has evaluated the entire situations, and the evidence on record

and arrived at a finding that the appellant has failed to

establish that she is entitled to a decree as sought for by her.

However, the Family Court has granted a decree for an amount

of Rs.40,000/- since the said amount is admitted by the

respondent as received from the appellant.

[p_42] 39. Therefore, we do not find any reason to interfere

with the partial decree passed by the Family Court for an

amount of Rs.40,000/-. However, in the body of the petition,

the Family Court has granted 9% interest to the said amount

of Rs.40,000/-, but at the relief portion, only 6% interest is

awarded. Taking into account the facts and circumstances, we

are of the opinion that the interest that was granted by the

Family Court to the said amount of Rs.40,000/- is at the rate

of 9% p.a. from 17.11.2011 till its realization. We order

Mat. Appeal No.68/2015 & conn. cases 40

accordingly. Therefore, the said appeal is dismissed, subject to

the above clarification and modification in the decree.
